paragraphs.text: Gyrate atrophy of the choroid and retina is an autosomal recessive chorioretinal degeneration caused by deficiency of ornithine-delta-aminotransferase (OAT), an enzyme of the mitochondrial matrix (Mitchell et al., 1988). Ornithine accumulates, and the chorioretinal degeneration is progressive (Wang et al., 2000). Balfoort et al. (2021) described GACR as a rare inborn error of amino acid metabolism. It is characterized by high plasma ornithine and by vision loss that begins early in life and eventually leads to complete blindness. No curative treatment exists.

paragraphs.text: Sipilä et al. (1979) studied 21 patients with gyrate atrophy of the choroid and retina and hyperornithinemia. The patients were not weak, but their type 2 muscle fibers were almost universally atrophic and contained tubular aggregates. The number of type 2 fibers decreased with age. Tubular aggregates occurred in both females and males, and the 2 sexes were affected equally. Gyrate atrophy was the first disease in which females were shown to have tubular aggregates.

paragraphs.text: Kaiser-Kupfer et al. (1983) described the cataract in 9 phakic patients with gyrate atrophy of the choroid and retina. By the second decade, cataract was a uniform finding. The opacities lay mainly along the confluence of the posterior sutures, where their position in the visual axis interfered with vision. The authors considered them unique compared with the cataracts seen in other forms of retinal degeneration. They also examined 3 lenses removed from patients aged 31 to 47 years. Histologically, the posterior suture region was filled with liquified, degenerated lens material typical of senile cataractous changes.

paragraphs.text: Valtonen et al. (1996) examined the thigh muscles of 7 patients with gyrate atrophy using semi-open conchotome muscle biopsies, CT, and ultralow-field MRI at 0.02 T. All biopsy samples showed type 2 muscle fiber atrophy, and 6 of the 7 had tubular aggregates. Muscle CT density was increased in the only child in the study, decreased in 3 elderly subjects, and normal in the remaining 3 patients. Mean T1 relaxation time of thigh muscle was lower in patients than in 6 healthy controls (135 vs 157 ms; p = 0.002), while T2 was slightly but not significantly increased. The authors concluded that thigh muscles of GA patients universally show changes on CT and MRI, but that relaxation time measurements gave little additional information on muscle metabolism.

paragraphs.text: Valtonen et al. (1999) studied central nervous system involvement in 23 untreated patients with gyrate atrophy, comparing them with age-matched healthy controls and with 9 patients who had received creatine or creatine precursor supplementation daily for several years. Brain MRI showed degenerative white matter lesions in 50% of patients and premature atrophic changes in 70%, with a striking increase in the number of Virchow spaces. Of the patients who had EEG recordings, 58% had abnormal slow background activity, focal lesions, or high-amplitude beta rhythm (more than 50 microV). EEG findings were not associated with MRI changes, age, or sex.

paragraphs.text: Peltola et al. (2002) looked for peripheral nervous system involvement in 40 patients with gyrate atrophy (mean age 31.6 +/- 16.3 years; range 5 to 74 years). Neurography was abnormal in 21 (53%), and these abnormalities were associated with patient age and with the severity of the ophthalmologic changes. Large-fiber sensory function was abnormal in 7 patients (18%) and small-fiber function in 4 (10%). Somatosensory and brainstem auditory evoked potentials were abolished in 5 patients. The authors concluded that gyrate atrophy is a systemic disease affecting both the central and the peripheral nervous system.

paragraphs.text: Wang et al. (1995) produced OAT-deficient mice by gene targeting. Unexpectedly, the newborn mice had hypoornithinemia and died as neonates, but short-term arginine supplementation rescued them. After weaning, the mice developed hyperornithinemia similar to that of human patients with gyrate atrophy. Over several months, they developed a retinal degeneration involving the photoreceptors and the pigment epithelium. The authors concluded that these mice appeared to be an excellent model of human gyrate atrophy.

paragraphs.text: Mitchell et al. (1988) studied 4 Lebanese patients with gyrate atrophy of the choroid and retina from 2 pedigrees. In the OAT gene, they found a G-to-A transition that changed the initiator ATG (methionine) codon to ATA. They first detected it as a probe-target mismatch at the 5-prime end of the first coding exon by RNase A protection, then confirmed it by sequencing. Zygosity was not stated. The mutation segregated with the disease allele in both pedigrees. If translation started at the nearest in-frame methionine codon, OAT would be shortened by 138 amino acids, removing the entire mitochondrial leader sequence and 113 amino acids of the mature peptide.
